questions.explain: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia in maternal diabetes inhibits surfactant synthesis, and caesarean without labour adds risk — so RDS can occur even near term. Chronic intrauterine stress (IUGR/pre-eclampsia) and prolonged rupture tend to accelerate lung maturation; antenatal steroids are protective.
questions.note: Prematurity (most important), maternal diabetes (fetal insulin), caesarean delivery.

questions.stem: An obstetrician considering delivery at 34 weeks obtains amniotic fluid; the lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio is 2.4. What does this indicate?
options: The result cannot be interpreted before 37 weeks
The fetal lungs are probably immature
Surfactant will be needed immediately after birth
The fetal lungs are probably mature
questions.explain: An L:S ratio ≥2 indicates mature lungs and low RDS risk (less reliable in maternal diabetes). A ratio <1.5 suggests immaturity.
questions.note: Mature lung: L:S ratio ≥ 2.

questions.stem: A 27-week baby on CPAP for RDS has recurrent apnoeas with bradycardia and desaturation. Sepsis screen is pending and he is on antibiotics. Which drug is most appropriate for the apnoeas?
questions.explain: Caffeine is the treatment of apnoea of prematurity and also reduces BPD. Antibiotics are continued until GBS/sepsis is excluded, because pneumonia can mimic RDS. Phenobarbital is for seizures; naloxone only for maternal opioid exposure.
questions.note: Caffeine for apnoea; antibiotics until GBS excluded; complications: NEC, ROP, BPD.

cards.front: Describe the pathophysiology of neonatal RDS.
cards.back: Prematurity → type II pneumocytes lack surfactant (mature ~35 wk) → high surface tension → small alveoli collapse (Laplace P = 2T/r) → atelectasis, hypoxaemia. Risk: prematurity, maternal diabetes, caesarean.

cards.front: What does the CXR show in RDS and how is lung maturity assessed?
cards.back: Ground-glass with air bronchograms, atelectasis, low lung volumes (BAD) • Mature lung: L:S ratio ≥2 • Onset within 4 h: tachypnoea, grunting, flaring, recession, cyanosis

cards.front: Outline prevention, treatment and complications of RDS.
cards.back: Antenatal glucocorticoids • CPAP from birth → surfactant if FiO₂ >0.30 • Caffeine for apnoea • Antibiotics until GBS excluded • Complications: NEC, ROP, BPD

II-35.summary: Meconium aspiration is a post-term, hypoxia-driven disease: ball-valve air trapping (pneumothorax), surfactant inactivation and PPHN — manage non-vigorous babies with prompt ventilation rather than routine tracheal suction, and escalate surfactant → iNO → ECMO.

questions.stem: A baby born at 42 weeks after an abnormal CTG has meconium-stained nails and cord and respiratory distress from birth. The chest looks barrel-shaped with widespread crackles. CXR shows coarse patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explain: Post-term, fetal distress, meconium staining, barrel chest and patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation = MAS. RDS gives low-volume ground-glass lungs in preterms; TTN gives fissure fluid; CDH gives a scaphoid abdomen and bowel loops in the chest.
questions.note: Meconium-stained skin/nails/cord; distress from birth; barrel chest, crackles.

questions.stem: A term baby is delivered through thick meconium-stained liquor. At birth he is floppy, apnoeic and has a heart rate of 80/min. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Suction the mouth and nose on the perineum first
Start positive-pressure ventilation within the first minute
Intubate and suction the trachea before any breaths
questions.explain: Current resuscitation guidance: for non-vigorous babies, no routine tracheal suctioning — start inflation breaths/ventilation within the first minute, because delaying ventilation worsens hypoxia. Intrapartum suctioning doesn't prevent MAS; tracheal suction is reserved for suspected airway obstruction.
questions.note: Non-vigorous baby: no routine tracheal suctioning; start ventilation within the first minute.

questions.stem: What is the main mechanism leading to in-utero passage of meconium?
options: Fetal hypoglycaemia triggering vagal inhibition of the gut
Maternal opioids relaxing the fetal anal sphincter
Fetal hypoxia increasing peristalsis and relaxing the anal sphincter
questions.explain: Fetal hypoxia (and gut maturity in post-term babies) increases peristalsis and relaxes the anal sphincter → meconium passage; hypoxic gasping then causes aspiration.
questions.note: Fetal hypoxia → increased peristalsis and anal sphincter relaxation → meconium passage → aspiration.

questions.stem: A term baby with MAS on CPAP suddenly deteriorates with worsening cyanosis. The left hemithorax appears hyperexpanded with reduced breath sounds, and the apex beat is displaced to the right. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: Meconium plugs act as ball valves, trapping air → air leak (pneumothorax in 10–20%). Unilateral hyperexpansion, reduced breath sounds and mediastinal shift point to tension pneumothorax needing needle decompression/drain. PPHN or prong displacement don't cause unilateral signs.
questions.note: Ball-valve air trapping → pneumothorax; meconium inactivates surfactant; PPHN.

questions.stem: A baby born at 30 weeks after maternal fever is covered in meconium-stained liquor. Which diagnosis should this specifically prompt?
questions.explain: Meconium passage is rare before 34 weeks; meconium in a preterm suggests Listeria chorioamnionitis (with maternal fever), so cover with amoxicillin/ampicillin. Post-maturity is the classic cause in term/post-term babies; Hirschsprung causes delayed meconium passage.
questions.note: Meconium in a preterm → think Listeria.

questions.stem: A term baby with MAS on high-frequency ventilation has labile oxygenation, with pre-ductal saturation 95% and post-ductal 80%. Echo shows a structurally normal heart with right-to-left ductal shunting. What is the most appropriate specific therapy?
questions.explain: The saturation gap with right-to-left ductal shunting indicates PPHN, treated with inhaled NO (selective pulmonary vasodilator) alongside oxygen, ventilation and surfactant. PGE1 keeps the duct open for duct-dependent heart disease; indometacin closes a PDA.
questions.note: NICU: oxygen, CPAP/ventilation, surfactant, inhaled nitric oxide for PPHN.

questions.stem: Why is exogenous surfactant often given to term infants with meconium aspiration syndrome?
options: Surfactant dissolves and clears meconium plugs
questions.explain: Meconium causes chemical pneumonitis and inactivates surfactant, producing secondary surfactant deficiency despite normal production at term. It doesn't dissolve plugs, and pulmonary vasoconstriction is treated with iNO.
questions.note: Ball-valve air trapping → pneumothorax; meconium inactivates surfactant; PPHN.

questions.stem: A term baby with severe MAS and PPHN remains profoundly hypoxaemic despite high-frequency ventilation, surfactant and inhaled nitric oxide. What is the next treatment option?
questions.explain: ECMO is the rescue therapy for refractory hypoxaemic respiratory failure in MAS/PPHN, with good survival. Antibiotics are given until sepsis is excluded. Exchange transfusion and lavage don't address PPHN; lung transplant is not a neonatal rescue option.
questions.note: ECMO if refractory; antibiotics until sepsis excluded.

cards.front: List the risk factors for meconium aspiration syndrome and a key exception.
cards.back: Post-term (postmaturity), growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, oligohydramnios, abnormal CTG • Meconium in a preterm → think Listeria

cards.front: Explain the pathophysiology of MAS.
cards.back: Fetal hypoxia → increased peristalsis + sphincter relaxation → meconium → aspiration • Ball-valve air trapping → pneumothorax (10–20%) • Meconium inactivates surfactant • PPHN (pre-/post-ductal gap)

cards.front: How do you manage meconium aspiration syndrome?
cards.back: Non-vigorous: no routine tracheal suctioning; ventilate within first minute • NICU: oxygen, CPAP/ventilation, surfactant, iNO for PPHN • ECMO if refractory • Antibiotics until sepsis excluded
